notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1205.tlg001.perseus-: In the first section τῆς ἀρχῇ ('their rule') looks corrupt; the sense is taken as 'their appointed rule'.

nodes.text: For the others, being free in their choice, as indeed they had been made by God, remained in the things for which God made and appointed them; but some outraged both the constitution of their being and their rule: both this ruler of matter and of the forms in it, and others of those about this first firmament (and know that we say nothing unattested, but report what has been proclaimed by the prophets); those fell into desire for virgins and were found weaker than the flesh, while this one became negligent and wicked in the management of what had been entrusted to him.

From those, then, who went after the virgins were born the so-called giants. And if something about the giants has been said in part by the poets too, do not be surprised: worldly wisdom and theological wisdom differ as much as truth differs from plausibility, the one being heavenly and the other earthly; and, in keeping with the ruler of matter, “we know how to tell many falsehoods like the truth.”

These angels, then, who fell from the heavens and keep about the air and the earth, no longer able to peer up into the realms above the heavens, together with the souls of the giants, are the demons who wander about the world, producing movements that match, the demons the natures they received, the angels the desires they conceived.

And the ruler of matter, as can be seen from the very things that happen, directs and governs in opposition to the goodness of God. “Often the thought has passed through my mind whether chance or a deity rules the affairs of life, bringing, against hope and against justice, some to fall from their homes without a livelihood, and others to prosper.”
And Neryllinus and Proteus and Alexander: what more do they do for the sick? For what the statue is now said to accomplish, it was accomplishing even while Neryllinus was alive and sick.
